title: D. B. Cooper: The Hijacker Who Jumped Into the Night and Vanished
case_meta: Portland to Reno, Pacific Northwest · November 1971
subject: cooper
description:
Do you think he survived the jump, or did the forest keep him? 👇

On the 24th of November 1971, a quiet man in a business suit hijacked Northwest Orient Flight 305, collected $200,000 and four parachutes in Seattle, and jumped from the back of a Boeing 727 somewhere over south-west Washington. This case file follows the flight, the 45-year FBI investigation known as NORJAK, the ransom money found on a Columbia River beach in 1980, and the particles on the tie he left behind.

Sources: FBI, "A Byte Out of History: D.B. Cooper" (2006) and Seattle field office statement (July 2016); Encyclopaedia Britannica, "D.B. Cooper"; HistoryLink.org, essay 23059 (2024); NBC News (2017); OPB (2021); Wikipedia, "D. B. Cooper" and its references.

scenes.text: At about thirteen minutes past eight on a November night in 1971, the tail of a Boeing 727 suddenly lifted, and the pilots had to trim the aircraft back to level.
Nobody in the cockpit saw what caused it. Behind them, the rear stairway under the tail had been hanging open in the dark for several minutes.
The only passenger left on board was a quiet man in a dark suit, with a bag of money tied around his waist and a parachute on his back.
When the plane landed in Reno almost three hours later, agents searched every row and every locker. The cabin was empty, and so was the sky behind it.
It is often called the only unsolved hijacking in the history of commercial aviation, and the man behind it is known by a name that was never really his.
The day before Thanksgiving, a man walked up to the Northwest Orient counter at Portland International Airport and paid cash for a one-way ticket to Seattle. He gave his name as Dan Cooper.
Witnesses later described him as a white man in his mid-forties, around six feet tall, with dark hair, brown eyes and a calm, unhurried manner.
He wore a business suit, a white shirt with a thin black clip-on tie, a raincoat and loafers. He carried a black attaché case and a brown paper bag.
Flight 305 was a short hop, about thirty minutes, on a Boeing 727. There were thirty-six passengers that afternoon, and a crew of six.
Captain William Scott and First Officer Bill Rataczak flew the plane, with Harold Anderson as flight engineer. Alice Hancock, Tina Mucklow and Florence Schaffner looked after the cabin.
Cooper took seat 18-E, in the last row of the cabin. Before takeoff he ordered a drink, bourbon with a mixer, and paid for it.
The aircraft pushed back on schedule at ten to three in the afternoon. A few minutes after takeoff, he pressed a folded slip of paper into Schaffner's hand.
She assumed it was a phone number and dropped it into her purse. Cooper leaned over and told her she had better read it, because he had a bomb.
The note was printed in neat capital letters with a felt-tip pen. It said he had a bomb in his briefcase, and that he wanted her to sit beside him.
He opened the case just enough for her to see a battery wired to red cylinders. Agents later thought they were probably road flares. Nobody on board could know that.
His demands went to the cockpit: two hundred thousand dollars in twenty-dollar bills, two main parachutes and two reserves, all waiting in Seattle by five o'clock.
The airline's president agreed to pay. The passengers were told about a minor mechanical problem, and the plane circled Puget Sound for about two hours while the money was gathered.
Seattle First National Bank produced ten thousand bills, weighing around nineteen pounds. FBI agents photographed their serial numbers before handing them over.
At 5:46 that evening, Flight 305 landed at Seattle-Tacoma. Mucklow carried the money and parachutes aboard, and Cooper let the other passengers walk off.
He kept the three men in the cockpit and Mucklow. His new instructions were precise: Mexico City, a fuel stop in Reno, ten thousand feet, about a hundred knots, landing gear down, rear door open.
At around twenty to eight, the 727 took off again and turned south. Military jets followed at a distance, flying slow S-shaped patterns to stay behind the airliner.
Before the jump, Mucklow helped lower the stairs and was sent forward to the cockpit. Cooper tied the money bag around his waist. She begged him to take the bomb with him.
The plane landed at Reno just after eleven. Agents lifted sixty-six latent fingerprints, eight cigarette butts, and two of the four parachutes. Cooper and the money were gone.
On seat 18-E lay his black clip-on tie, with a gold tie clip set with mother-of-pearl. The FBI traced it to J. C. Penney, which had stopped selling that model in 1968.
The bureau called the case NORJAK, for Northwest Hijacking. Within five years it had looked at more than eight hundred suspects and set aside all but about two dozen.
Early on, a reporter rushing to meet a deadline wrote the name down as D. B. Cooper. Other outlets repeated it, and the mistake has stuck for more than half a century.
Investigators worked out a likely drop zone near the town of Ariel, around Lake Merwin. In the spring of 1972, soldiers from Fort Lewis walked those woods for eighteen days at a time.
A Navy submarine searched the lake to a depth of two hundred feet. Nobody found a parachute, a body, or a single bill.
In November 1978, a deer hunter picked up a sign near a logging road east of Castle Rock. It was the instruction placard for the rear stairs of a 727.
On the 10th of February 1980, an eight-year-old named Brian Ingram was raking sand for a campfire on a beach called Tena Bar, on the Washington side of the Columbia River.
He uncovered three crumbling bundles of twenty-dollar bills, still held together by rubber bands. Two packets held a hundred bills each. The third held ninety.
That came to five thousand eight hundred dollars. The serial numbers matched the ransom, and the bills were still in the same order the bank had packed them.
The find made no sense to anyone. Tena Bar lies about twenty miles from Ariel, near Vancouver, Washington, well away from the drop zone the FBI had spent years searching.
Money scattered by a falling man would not stay in neat bundles with rubber bands. Someone, or the river, had carried those packets there.
Later digs on the beach turned up nothing else. Of the two hundred thousand dollars, ten thousand bills, only these two hundred and ninety have ever been found.
The FBI has never stated an official position on whether Cooper survived. The agents who worked the case have disagreed openly with each other for decades.
Larry Carr, who led the team from 2006 to 2009, believed he died that night, and said Cooper probably never even got his parachute open.
Carr's argument was practical. The main parachutes could not be steered. Cooper jumped at night, in loafers and a raincoat, into thick forest.
And one of the reserves was a training dummy, its canopy sewn shut. An experienced skydiver would probably have noticed. Investigators concluded that Cooper was no expert.
Others in the bureau thought he made it. One senior Seattle agent told a newspaper in 1976 that he believed Cooper had got away, and the money found in 1980 never settled the question.

Some researchers have argued that Richard McCoy was Cooper. He carried out a very similar hijacking less than five months later. The FBI ruled him out, saying he did not match the flight attendants' descriptions.
The tie offered a different trail. In 2017, a group of volunteer scientists found particles of cerium, strontium sulfide and pure, unalloyed titanium on it.
They suggested its owner may have worked at a plant that made metal for the aerospace industry. The FBI never said whether it agreed, and nobody knows for certain the tie was even his.
On the 8th of July 2016, the FBI announced that it would no longer actively investigate the case, after forty-five years, and move its resources to more urgent work.
The bureau said that no tip and no new technology had produced the proof it needed to charge anyone beyond a reasonable doubt.
The evidence went to FBI headquarters in Washington. The bureau still asks anyone who finds something linked to the parachutes or the money to bring it in.
Amateur searchers still return to the Columbia River beaches and the woods around Lake Merwin with shovels, metal detectors and their own theories.

The most cautious answer is also the least satisfying. He most likely died in the forest, and the river moved part of the money. The more than nine thousand seven hundred missing bills prove nothing either way.
What the record shows is a short list of hard facts: a ticket, a tie, a sign from a stairway, and two hundred and ninety rotting bills.
Everything else comes back to that small jolt in the cockpit at thirteen minutes past eight, when the tail lifted, a man stepped into the dark, and the story of D. B. Cooper began.
